title: Ilfa, Called Chilfai in the Jerusalem Talmud
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.
copyright: English translation and editorial notes © 2026 Joshua Waxman. All rights reserved.
paragraphs: Hyman considers it clear that Ilfa is Chilfa, for in Temurah 28a, “Ilfa asked: He said, ‘On the gleanings when they fall,’” etc., and in Terumot, chapter 6, end of halakhah 2, the reading is Chilfai. Likewise the incident cited in Taanit 21a, where a certain elder asked Ilfa, is found in Kiddushin 1:1, with the additional locator ד, as Chilfai.

He was already great in Rabbi’s days, as in Taanit 24a: Rabbi decreed a fast and rain did not come. Ilfa — and some say Rabbi Ilfi (Dikdukei Soferim: Rabbi Ilfa) — went down before him; he said “Who causes the wind to blow,” and a wind blew … Rabbi asked him, “What is your deed?” He told him that he lived in a village where they had no wine for kiddush and havdalah, and he would take the trouble to bring wine and fulfill their obligation for them. He was Rabbi Yochanan’s colleague, although, in Hyman’s reconstruction, he was much older than Rabbi Yochanan, as related in Taanit 21b [supplied locator; see note]: Ilfa and Rabbi Yochanan were studying Torah, and they were in great distress. They said, “Let us rise and go and do business.” They went and sat under a ruined wall and sat down to eat. Two ministering angels came; Rabbi Yochanan heard one say to the other, “Let us throw this wall on them and kill them, for they leave eternal life …” The other said to him, “Leave them, for there is one whose hour stands ready for him.” Rabbi Yochanan heard this, and not Ilfa. Rabbi Yochanan returned, and Ilfa went to trade. By the time Ilfa came [back], Rabbi Yochanan had become king [head]. They said to Ilfa: “Had the Master sat and studied, would the Master not have become king?” (and as we said, he was much older than Rabbi Yochanan). He answered them that nevertheless he had not forgotten his learning, and whoever asked him a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya or Rabbi Oshaya and he could not resolve it from our Mishnah, he would throw himself into the sea. A certain elder came and asked him, and he answered everything properly. The incident is likewise cited briefly in the Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Ketubot, chapter 6, and in Kiddushin 1:1, with the additional locator ד., at length, with several questions they asked him, and there it is Chilfai.

Likewise we find that Rabbi Yochanan spoke in his name, as in Zevachim 20a, “Rabbi Yochanan said: Ilfa asked,” and there, 21a, “Rabbi Yochanan said in Ilfa’s name”; in Shabbat 17:3, “Rabbi Yochanan said: Chilfai took me [to show me]”; and at the end of Terumot, chapter 1, and Challah, chapter 2, end of halakhah 2, “Rabbi Yochanan said: I brought it from Chilfai’s.” Their dispute is in Zevachim 29b, and we likewise find that he asked Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, as in Nazir 6:10. His sayings we find in Shabbat 14b, Ketubot 111a, Bava Kamma 20a and Chullin 32b and 53b. Of those who speak in his name we find Rabbi Elazar, Maaserot 2:4;

Rabbi Chanin bar Ami, Eruvin 67a according to Dikdukei Soferim; and Rabbi Yirmeyah, Bava Metzia 114b. Hyman considers it very likely that he too composed baraitot, and this is what we find in Menachot 70a, “It is written in Ilfa’s notebook: Eggs of a bird carcass,” etc.; and in Maaserot 2:4, “Rabbi Yonah said: I found it written in Chilfai’s notebook: One who eats,” etc.

notes.text: The name-equivalence, age comparison and baraita-authorship conjecture are Hyman’s, with their original strength retained. The Kiddushin source has כ״א ה״א and additional ד/ד.; 1:1 is an interpretation of the chapter/halakhah abbreviation, while the additional locator remains literal rather than an established page-side conversion. מחלקיתן is interpreted as מחלוקתן. The second Taanit citation is supplied כא: (21b), although the saved Davidson21a paragraphs2–7 contain the connected Ilfa/Yochanan wall and academy episode; the whole saved21b scalar has no Ilfa. Both supplied and matching locations are retained. Guggenheimer JTShabbat17:3 Hebrew paragraph2 continues משכני חילפיי with והראני נגר: Chilfai took Yochanan to show him a bolt, so pulled me is clarified contextually without changing the abbreviated quotation into a separate teaching.

The complete consulted Taanit 21a sequence has Ilfa and Yochanan under the wall, Yochanan alone hearing the angels, their different decisions, Yochanan’s academy leadership, and Ilfa’s boat challenge and answer to the elder. Hyman’s second citation supplies 21b and is retained. The direct story does not prove that Ilfa was much older or independently establish every Ilfa/Chilfai identification. Hyman’s name-equivalence conclusion keeps its clear force, and the notebook-authorship proposal remains very likely in his argument. The extra Kiddushin locator ד remains literal; the exact Dikdukei Soferim reading and the broader reporting-chain comparisons remain attributed.
